explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. David says the LORD lifted him up and "have not allowed my foes to rejoice over me." (Psalm 30:1) His enemies wanted a party, and the LORD canceled the invitations.

Good guess, since David was king of Israel. But the psalm never mentions a crown. David says the LORD "have not allowed my foes to rejoice over me." (Psalm 30:1) The answer is rejoicing, and the foes didn't get any.

I can see why a baker would pick that, because foes sound like trouble. But this verse says nothing about a city or a fire. David says the LORD "have not allowed my foes to rejoice over me." (Psalm 30:1) No victory party for them.
Yes, healed. David says, "O LORD my God, I cried to You for help, and You healed me." (Psalm 30:2) He cried out, and the LORD answered. I like those odds.
Crowned sounds royal, and David was a king. But the verse says something else: "I cried to You for help, and You healed me." (Psalm 30:2) The LORD healed him.
Armed would fit a king who has foes. But David doesn't say that here. He says, "I cried to You for help, and You healed me." (Psalm 30:2) Healing is what he got.
Right, baker. David says, "You pulled me up from Sheol; You spared me from descending into the Pit." (Psalm 30:3) He was headed down, and the LORD pulled him back up.
A kingdom is a big thing to lose, but David doesn't say it here. He says the LORD pulled him up from Sheol and "spared me from descending into the Pit." (Psalm 30:3) The Pit is the answer.
Exile is a reasonable guess, but it isn't in this verse. David says, "You spared me from descending into the Pit." (Psalm 30:3) The LORD pulled him up from Sheol, and that's where his focus stays.
Fleeting is the word, baker. David says, "For His anger is fleeting, but His favor lasts a lifetime." (Psalm 30:5) One passes quickly and the other lasts a lifetime. Easy math.
Endless gets the sentence backward. David says, "For His anger is fleeting, but His favor lasts a lifetime." (Psalm 30:5) It's His favor that lasts a lifetime.

Hidden is close to something David does say a couple of verses later, about the LORD hiding His face. But in verse 5 the word is fleeting: "For His anger is fleeting, but His favor lasts a lifetime." (Psalm 30:5) Anger passes quickly and favor lasts.
Joy, baker. David says, "Weeping may stay the night, but joy comes in the morning." (Psalm 30:5) The weeping has to leave at some point.
Rest sounds nice after a long night of weeping. But David says, "Weeping may stay the night, but joy comes in the morning." (Psalm 30:5) What comes is joy.
Quiet would be peaceful, but it isn't what David says. He says, "Weeping may stay the night, but joy comes in the morning." (Psalm 30:5) Joy is what arrives.

That's it. David says, "In prosperity I said, 'I will never be shaken.'" (Psalm 30:6) Things were going well, and he talked like nothing could touch him. I bet most of us have said something like that.
David did spend time in the wilderness, but that's not when he says this. The verse reads, "In prosperity I said, 'I will never be shaken.'" (Psalm 30:6) He said it when life was going well.
You'd think a sickbed would humble a person, not make him brag. David says, "In prosperity I said, 'I will never be shaken.'" (Psalm 30:6) It was the good times that made him talk that way.

True, baker. David says, "You favored me; You made my mountain stand strong. When You hid Your face, I was dismayed." (Psalm 30:7) The mountain was strong, and then he was dismayed. I think that's a lot to take in.
It's actually true. David says, "O LORD, You favored me; You made my mountain stand strong. When You hid Your face, I was dismayed." (Psalm 30:7) Strong mountain first, then he was dismayed.

explanations.answer: If he dies he can't praise the LORD
explanations.explanation: You've got it, baker. David asks, "What gain is there in my bloodshed, in my descent to the Pit? Will the dust praise You? Will it proclaim Your faithfulness?" (Psalm 30:9) He wants to be alive to praise the LORD. That's a good reason to ask for help.

explanations.answer: Even dust will praise the LORD someday
explanations.explanation: That's an interesting twist, but it isn't what David means. He asks, "Will the dust praise You? Will it proclaim Your faithfulness?" (Psalm 30:9) He's asking about the Pit, and the point is that he wants to be alive to praise the LORD.

explanations.answer: His foes are worth no more than dust
explanations.explanation: His foes did come up at the start of the psalm, so I see the connection. But this verse isn't about them. David asks, "What gain is there in my bloodshed, in my descent to the Pit? Will the dust praise You?" (Psalm 30:9) He's talking about his own going down to the Pit and the praise that would go with him.

Joy, baker. David says, "You turned my mourning into dancing; You peeled off my sackcloth and clothed me with joy." (Psalm 30:11) The LORD took off the sackcloth and gave him something better to wear. Best outfit change ever.
Armor makes sense for a king with foes. But David says, "You peeled off my sackcloth and clothed me with joy." (Psalm 30:11) What he got dressed in was joy, not armor.
Linen is a fair guess, since we're talking about clothing. But David says, "You peeled off my sackcloth and clothed me with joy." (Psalm 30:11) It was joy, not fabric.

explanations.answer: So his heart would sing and not be silent
explanations.explanation: Yes. David says the LORD did it "that my heart may sing Your praises and not be silent." (Psalm 30:12) The turning-around has a point: a heart that sings.

explanations.answer: So his foes would see it and be ashamed
explanations.explanation: Foes are in this psalm, but not in this verse. David says the LORD turned his mourning into dancing "that my heart may sing Your praises and not be silent." (Psalm 30:12) The reason he gives is his own singing heart.

explanations.answer: So the people would follow him to battle
explanations.explanation: David was a king, so a battle isn't a crazy guess. But the psalm gives a different reason: "that my heart may sing Your praises and not be silent." (Psalm 30:12) It's about singing, not marching.

I get why that sounds right, since David has been through a lot. But he says, "O LORD my God, I will give thanks forever." (Psalm 30:12) Forever has no troubles-are-over deadline on it. The answer is False.
False is right, baker. David ends with, "O LORD my God, I will give thanks forever." (Psalm 30:12) He doesn't set an end date, and forever means forever.
